items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the family court act, in relation to requiring attorneys for children to receive training or education in domestic violence prevention; to amend the domestic relations law, in relation to requiring the court to state on the record the domestic violence and child abuse factored into their award of custody or visitation; to amend the criminal procedure law and the family court act, in relation to orders of protection; and to amend the criminal procedure law, in relation to reporting domestic violence incidents to the supervising probation department or the division of parole
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:A9017

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the family court act, in relation to
requiring attorneys for children to receive training or education in
domestic violence prevention; to amend the domestic relations law, in
relation to requiring the court to state on the record the domestic
violence and child abuse factored into their award of custody or visita-
tion; to amend the criminal procedure law and the family court act, in
relation to orders of protection; and to amend the criminal procedure
law, in relation to reporting domestic violence incidents to the super-
vising probation department or the division of parole

Purpose:  This bill would: (1) require education and training on the
effects of domestic violence for court-appointed attorneys for children;
(2) require courts to state on the record how established incidents of
domestic violence and child abuse factored into determinations of visi-
tation or custody; (3) authorize concurrent jurisdiction in family court
for certain sex offenses; (4) provide for transmission of domestic
violence incident reports involving probationers or parolees to the
relevant agency as soon as practicable; (5) provide that records be made
available to law enforcement when there is a conviction of the violation
of harassment in the second degree against a member of the same family
or household; and (6) provide for extending of an order of protection
during a period of incarceration.

Summary of Provisions:  Section 1 of the bill would amend Family Court
Act (FCA) § 249-b to require the chief administrator of the courts to
promulgate rules to provide that each person appointed to be an attorney
for a child shall complete a training program, which would include the
effects of domestic violence on children and the relationship between
domestic violence and custody, visitation and child support. Such a
training program would be developed with the input of and in consulta-
tion with the Office for the Prevention of Domestic Violence.

Section 2 of the bill would amend Domestic Relations Law (DRL)
240(1)(a) to require that, where allegations of domestic violence or
child abuse are raised and established by a preponderance of the
evidence, a court must state on the record how findings, facts and
circumstances of domestic violence or child abuse factored into the
court's determination of custody or visitation.

Sections 3, 4, and 5 of the bill would amend Criminal Procedure Law
(CPL) § 530.11(1), FCA § 812(1) and FCA § 821(1)(a), respectively, to
add the crimes of sexual misconduct, forcible touching, sexual abuse in
the third degree and sexual abuse in the second degree as set forth in
Penal Law § 130.60(1) to those family offenses for which a victim may
obtain an order of protection in family court, and subjecting these
offenses to mandatory arrest and reporting requirements of CPL § 140.10.

Section 6 of the bill would amend CPL § 140.10(5) to provide that a
report of a domestic violence incident involving an individual known by
the law enforcement officer to be under probation or parole supervision

must be transmitted by the officer to the supervising probation or
parole agency as soon as practicable.

Sections 7 and 8 of the bill would amend CPL § 160.55(1)(a) and CPL
160.55(1)(d), respectively, to provide that palmprints and fingerprints
concerning an arrest for harassment in the second degree against a
member of the same family or household will be retained and that records
and papers of arrest and prosecution may be made available to certain
qualified agencies in cases in which the defendant is convicted of
harassment in the second degree against a member of the same family or
household.

Section 9 of the bill would amend CPL § 170.10(4) to add a new paragraph
(e) to provide that the Court inform the defendant that the records and
papers in the arrest and prosecution of a conviction of harassment in
the second degree against a member of the same family or household shall
be accessible for law enforcement purposes.

Section 10 of the bill would amend CPL § 160.55(2) to provide that when
a defendant has been found guilty of harassment in the second degree
against a member of the same family or household, the clerk of the court
shall include notification of such disposition to the Division of Crimi-
nal Justice Services.

Section 11 of the bill would amend CPL § 170.10 by adding a new subdivi-
sion 8-a to provide notice to a defendant that he or she was alleged to
have committed harassment in the second degree against a member of the
same family or household and creates a procedure for determining if the
offense was committed against a member of the same family or household.

Sections 12 and 13 of the bill would amend CPL § 530.12(5) and CPL
530.13(4), respectively, to provide that, upon conviction of a class A
misdemeanor and issuance of an order of protection, such order of
protection may be extended during the period of the defendant's incar-
ceration.

Section 14 of the bill would provide that, consistent with available
resources, the Division of Human Rights shall develop training programs
in conjunction with the Office for the Prevention of Domestic Violence
to implement certain changes to the Human Rights Law.

Section 15 of the bill would provide that it shall take effect 90 days
after enactment; however sections 7, 8, and 10 would take effect in 120
days and apply to convictions on and after such date and sections 9 and
11 would take effect 30 days after enactment.

Existing Law:  FCA § 249-b requires the chief administrator of courts to
promulgate court rules prescribing workload standards for attorneys for
children.

DRL § 240(1) requires that, with respect to child custody or visitation
determinations in matrimonial actions, where allegations of domestic

violence or child abuse are established by a preponderance of the
evidence, courts must consider the effects of such domestic violence or
child abuse in making the custody or visitation determination.

CPL § 530.11 provides that criminal court and family court shall have
concurrent jurisdiction over certain crimes, including, for example,
disorderly conduct, harassment, menacing and stalking, when the crime is
committed between members of the same family or household.

FCA § 812 provides that family court and criminal court shall have
concurrent jurisdiction over certain crimes, including, for example,
disorderly conduct, harassment, menacing and stalking, when the crime is
committed between members of the same family or household.

FCA § 821 provides that a family offense proceeding may commence upon
the filing of a petition alleging, that a respondent engaged in certain
criminal conduct against a household or family member, including, for
example, disorderly conduct, harassment, stalking and menacing.

CPL § 140.10(4) provides that a law enforcement officer must arrest an
individual where the officer has reasonable cause to believe he or she
has committed an offense enumerated in CPL § 530.11(1) against a member
of the same family or household.

CPL § 140.10(5) provides that a law enforcement officer must prepare and
file a written report of a crime between members of the same family or
household, whether or not an arrest is made.

CPL § 160.55 provides that, where a criminal action or proceeding has
been terminated against a defendant by way of the defendant's conviction
of a traffic infraction or violation, other than certain enumerated
violations, records of such criminal action or proceeding shall be
sealed.

CPL § 530.12(5) provides for the issuance and maximum duration of orders
of protection issued in family offense cases.

CPL § 530.13(4) provides for the issuance and maximum duration of orders
of protection in cases other than family offenses.

Justification:  Domestic violence is a crime of enormous magnitude that
affects all New Yorkers-regardless of age, race, or economic status-with
long term and pervasive consequences for victims, families, communities
and society. Each year, an estimated 400,000 domestic violence incidents
are reported to law enforcement in New York, and approximately 300,000
calls are received by hotlines throughout the State. Nearly 165,000
orders of protection were issued in domestic violence cases in family,
criminal and supreme courts in 2007 alone.

In New York and around the nation, several high profile domestic
violence cases have renewed focus on the effects of domestic violence on
victims, children and our communities. In addition, some studies have

indicated an increased risk of abusive conduct during difficult finan-
cial times. The stresses of an economic downturn might also make it more
difficult for victims of domestic violence to take the steps they need
to get and stay safe.

While New York vigorously responds to domestic violence, with over 550
police departments, 200 emergency rooms, 150 domestic violence service
providers, 99 domestic violence hotlines and 1,000 specialized courts,
improvements can be made to hold offenders accountable, support victims
of domestic violence and protect our children from exposure to and
involvement in domestic violence situations. This bill will implement
legislative changes that will strengthen New York's support for victims
and their children while holding offenders accountable.

* Protecting Children from Harmful Exposure to Domestic Violence

Children exposed to domestic violence often suffer psychological, behav-
ioral and academic challenges. In 1996, the legislature recognized the
harmful effects of domestic violence on children and established domes-
tic violence as a factor that courts must consider in child custody and
visitation proceedings. Thirteen years later, studies indicate that the
presence of domestic violence often has little impact on custody and
visitation determinations. This bill would require courts to state on
the record how the findings, facts and circumstances of domestic
violence or child abuse were factored into the custody or visitation
determination, where such abuse was established by a preponderance of
the evidence. In addition, this bill would require that attorneys for
children be trained on the dynamics of domestic violence so they can
better counsel and represent their clients.

* Holding Offenders Accountable

New York recognizes certain crimes as offenses that may be committed
within a family setting, and enumerates those offenses in FCA § 812.
When a crime is recognized as a family offense, victims are eligible to
petition for orders of protection in family court. These orders of
protection are listed on a state-wide registry and the police must
arrest an individual where there is reasonable cause to believe that the
individual has committed a designated family offense. Currently, New
York does not include sex crimes within those designated as "family
offenses," even though there is a high correlation between domestic
violence and sexual assault. This bill would allow evidence of certain
sex crimes committed against members of the same family or household to
be heard in family court order of protection proceedings, while ensuring
that mandatory arrest applies and that orders of protection are filed
with the statewide registry.

Law enforcement is not currently required to notify supervisory agen-
cies, such as the supervising probation department or the New York State
Division of Parole, when a probationer or parolee is involved in a
domestic incident. Law enforcement officers are required to complete a
domestic incident report when they respond to any domestic call. This

bill would require the law enforcement officer to transmit a domestic
incident report to the supervisory probation department or New York
State Division of Parole when the alleged abuser is known to be on
probation or parole. Since such supervising agencies frequently impose
the condition that a probationer or parolee report any contact with law
enforcement, this bill would assist the agencies in enforcing this
condition, thereby ensuring that offenders are held accountable.

Most domestic violence cases are initially charged as misdemeanors, but
many ultimately plead down to harassment charges, which are violations
and subject to sealing. This process prohibits law enforcement from
accessing the records and papers pertaining to these convictions result-
ing in limited access to information crucial to charging decisions, such
as whether an offense was part of a course of conduct and who was the
primary aggressor. This bill would allow a defendant to obtain a non-
criminal disposition, when all parties deem that outcome to be appropri-
ate, while ensuring that law enforcement has a complete understanding of
the nature of the domestic violence history for any future incidents.

Orders of protection are crucial to the safety of victims. It is impor-
tant that these protections be made available while a defendant is
incarcerated and upon release. This bill provides greater protections to
victims by adding the length of incarceration to the maximum expiration
date previously allowed for orders of protections issued in misdemeanor
and violation cases.

Budgetary Implications:  This bill is not expected to have a material
impact on State finances.

Effective Date:  This bill would take effect 90 days after it becomes a
law; provided that sections 7, 8 and 10 would take effect 120 days after
enactment and apply to convictions on and after that date and sections 9
and 11 would take effect 30 days after enactment.

summary: Requires lawyers for children to receive training or education in domestic violence; requires the court to state on the record the domestic violance and child abuse factored into their award of custody or visitation.
title: Enacts provisions relating to domestic violence; requiring attorneys for children to receive training or education in domestic violence
